actions.justification: ★ MANDATORY: Assessing hydration status is critical in this CKD stage 4 diabetic patient prior to contrast administration. Adequate pre-procedural hydration is the cornerstone of CIN prevention.
★ MANDATORY: Baseline eGFR must be established in this CKD stage 4 patient to quantify renal risk prior to contrast exposure and guide pre-procedural nephroprotective strategies.

★ MANDATORY: Reviewing all risk factors (CKD, diabetes, possible heart failure, medication use) is essential to stratify CIN risk and plan appropriate preventive measures before cardiac catheterization.
Establish current hemodynamic baseline prior to contrast exposure in this high-risk CKD stage 4 diabetic patient undergoing cardiac catheterization.
Review current medications to identify nephrotoxins (NSAIDs, metformin, ACE inhibitors) that may need to be held prior to contrast administration in a CKD stage 4 patient.
Calculate the maximum safe contrast volume limit based on eGFR and body weight to minimize contrast-induced nephropathy risk in this high-risk patient (CKD stage 4 + diabetes).

Patient has CKD stage 4 and diabetes, both high-risk for contrast-induced nephropathy. Before proceeding with contrast for cardiac catheterization, consider whether alternative imaging (e.g., CO2 angiography, MRI) could reduce or eliminate contrast exposure.
CKD stage 4 with diabetes represents very high risk for contrast-induced AKI. Nephrology consultation is warranted to optimize pre-procedural management and guide contrast minimization strategies.
Review and hold any nephrotoxic medications (NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, metformin) prior to contrast administration to reduce additive renal injury risk in this high-risk patient.

Patient has CKD stage 4 and is planned for cardiac catheterization with contrast exposure. Documenting baseline eGFR is critical for contrast-induced nephropathy risk stratification and post-procedure monitoring planning.

Patient with CKD stage 4 and diabetes is at high risk for contrast-induced AKI. Nephrotoxic medications (NSAIDs, metformin, ACE inhibitors if applicable) should be held prior to contrast administration per CI-AKI prevention guidelines.

Baseline urine output assessment in a CKD stage 4 diabetic patient prior to contrast exposure helps guide pre-procedural hydration strategy and establishes a baseline for post-procedure AKI surveillance.
Patient has diabetes and is on metformin. Per guidelines, metformin should be held before contrast administration in CKD stage 4 patients due to risk of lactic acidosis if AKI develops post-contrast.

IV crystalloid (isotonic saline or sodium bicarbonate) hydration is the cornerstone of CI-AKI prevention in high-risk patients (CKD stage 4 + diabetes). Should be initiated pre-procedure to optimize renal perfusion.
Post-contrast SCr monitoring at 48 hours is required to detect contrast-induced AKI, defined as >0.3 mg/dL rise or >50% increase from baseline, per nephrology and CI-AKI guidelines.
Patient has CKD stage 4 and diabetes with planned contrast exposure — holding nephrotoxic medications is critical to reduce risk of contrast-induced nephropathy.
Pre- and post-procedure IV hydration with isotonic crystalloid is a cornerstone of CI-AKI prevention in high-risk patients (CKD stage 4, diabetes).

Patient has CKD stage 4 (likely eGFR <30-44), placing them at G3b or worse; metformin should be held peri-procedure to prevent lactic acidosis in the setting of potential contrast-induced renal deterioration.

Patient has CKD stage 4 and diabetes, both major risk factors for contrast-induced nephropathy. Pre-procedure IV hydration with isotonic crystalloid is a cornerstone of CI-AKI prevention per guidelines.
Ongoing urine output monitoring is essential in this high-risk patient (CKD stage 4, diabetes) undergoing contrast exposure to detect early signs of acute kidney injury.
Serial serum creatinine checks at 48-72 hours post-contrast are recommended to identify contrast-induced AKI, especially critical in this patient with significantly reduced baseline renal function.

Patient with CKD stage 4 and diabetes undergoing cardiac catheterization with contrast exposure requires serial creatinine monitoring. 72-hour post-contrast SCr check is essential to detect contrast-induced nephropathy, especially given high-risk comorbidities.

Patient has CKD stage 4 and diabetes — high risk for contrast-induced nephropathy. Nephrology input is warranted for ongoing renal protection strategy, potential need for RRT planning, and post-procedure management.
Optimizing fluid status is critical in CKD stage 4 patients undergoing contrast procedures to minimize nephrotoxic risk. Ensures adequate renal perfusion without fluid overload.
